meta.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This is a plain-English summary of the platforms' public policy pages, kept for marketing planning, and platforms change their rules often. Check the platform's live page, your state bar's rules and your own counsel before you run an ad.

summary: The ad-platform policies that affect US law-firm advertising on Google Ads, Google Local Services, YouTube, Microsoft Ads, Meta, LinkedIn and ChatGPT ads: what each rule says in plain English, what a firm should do about it, which practice areas it touches, when it took effect, and a dated log of changes. Each record quotes the platform's own policy or help page and gives the date it was read.

records.policyName: Legal requirements (no standalone legal-services policy)
records.rule: Google Ads has no policy written just for lawyers. Law-firm ads follow the general policies, and Google expects you to follow the law in every place your ads show, which includes your state bar's ad rules.
records.whatToDo: Check your state's lawyer-ad rules before launch. Then check the practice-specific Google rules in this table (bail, government documents, debt, drug names, sensitive audiences).
records.quote: You're required to comply with the local laws and regulations of any area your ads target, in addition to Google Ads policies.

records.policyName: Other restricted businesses: Government documents and services (October 2026 update)
records.rule: Since October 5, 2026, only governments and 'authorized providers' may run ads that promote getting a government document or service. To count as authorized, a government website must link to your domain and name you as authorized for that document or service.
records.whatToDo: Write ads about legal advice and representation, not about getting the visa, card, benefit or number itself. If an ad is disapproved, use Google's exclusion form to say you don't promote government documents.
records.quote: your domain must be linked from an official, publicly accessible government website and explicitly referenced as authorized

records.policyName: Government documents and services: are law firms in scope?
records.rule: Google's 2020 version of this policy said legal services and consultation-focused immigration lawyers were not restricted. The current policy page and the October 2026 notice don't repeat that exemption. Whether a given law-firm ad is caught is Google's call.
records.whatToDo: If a legal-services ad is disapproved under this policy, apply for exclusion with the option 'I am not promoting government documents and services'. That route needs Google's advertiser verification. Keep the 2020 text handy for the appeal.

records.policyName: Government documents and services: automatic 'Not a government website' label
records.rule: Google adds a 'Not a government website' label to Search ads it treats as promoting government documents or services, unless the advertiser is certified as a government provider.
records.whatToDo: Expect the label on immigration and benefits ads that Google treats as in scope. Make sure your landing page also says plainly that you are a private law firm.

records.policyName: Other restricted businesses: Bail bond services
records.rule: Ads for bail bond services are not allowed. Google's examples include immigration bail services and detention bail services.
records.whatToDo: Advertise legal representation, bond hearings handled by a lawyer and case defense. Don't offer to post or finance bail.
records.quote: Promotion of bail bonds services that offer to act as surety in order to secure bail for a defendant is not allowed.

records.text: Ads for bail bond services are not allowed. Google's examples include immigration bail services and detention bail services.

records.policyName: Financial products and services: Debt services (US)
records.rule: In the US, Google allows debt settlement and debt management ads only from approved non-profit credit counseling agencies, and only after certification. The policy doesn't mention bankruptcy lawyers.
records.whatToDo: Keep bankruptcy ads about Chapter 7 and 13 representation. Avoid 'settle your debt' or 'lower your payments' offers, which read like debt settlement or management.
records.quote: Google allows ads promoting debt services only if the advertiser and provider of these services is an approved non-profit budget and credit counseling agency

sources.label: Google Ads policy: Debt services
sources.quote: Google allows ads promoting debt services only if the advertiser and provider of these services is an approved non-profit budget and credit counseling agency

records.note: Federal law (11 U.S.C. §528) separately requires the debt-relief-agency statement in bankruptcy ads; that's a legal rule, not a Google rule.
records.text: In the US, Google allows debt settlement and debt management ads only from approved non-profit credit counseling agencies, and only after certification. The policy doesn't mention bankruptcy lawyers.

records.policyName: Financial products and services: Credit repair services
records.rule: Ads for credit repair services are not allowed on Google, including from lead generators.
records.whatToDo: Don't offer to 'fix' or 'repair' credit in ads. Consumer-protection firms (FCRA disputes) should describe the legal claim, not credit repair.
records.quote: Ads for credit repair services are not allowed.

sources.label: Google Ads policy: Financial products and services

records.note: Whether an FCRA lawsuit ad is treated as credit repair is Google's call (U).
records.text: Ads for credit repair services are not allowed on Google, including from lead generators.

records.policyName: Financial products and services: Loan modification
records.rule: Loan modification and foreclosure ads are disapproved if they guarantee results or charge an upfront fee. The upfront-fee ban has an exception when a law firm provides the service.
records.whatToDo: Foreclosure-defense firms can mention their fee structure, but never promise to stop a foreclosure or win a modification.
records.quote: Charging an upfront fee, unless service is being provided by a law firm

records.policyName: Healthcare and medicines: Restricted drug terms
records.rule: In the US you may use prescription drug names in ad text and landing pages without certification, but you must be certified by Google to keyword-target those drug names.
records.whatToDo: Before bidding on '[drug] lawsuit' keywords, ask Google whether you need healthcare certification. Don't assume a lawsuit keyword is exempt.

records.policyName: Personalized advertising: Commission of a crime
records.rule: Criminal defense lawyers are a named example of a sensitive interest category. Their ads can't use advertiser-curated audiences: Customer Match, your data segments (remarketing), audience expansion or lookalike segments. Google's own audiences (in-market, affinity, life events) are allowed.
records.whatToDo: Run criminal-defense campaigns on keywords, location and Google's predefined audiences. Remove remarketing and Customer Match lists from those campaigns.

records.policyName: Personalized advertising: Health
records.rule: Personal health content is a sensitive interest category. Google's definition includes disabilities and invasive medical procedures. Ads that fall in it can't use advertiser-curated audiences.
records.whatToDo: Expect disability, medical-malpractice and drug-injury ads to be treated as health-sensitive. Plan them without remarketing or Customer Match.

records.policyName: Personalized advertising: Abuse and trauma
records.rule: A person's status as a victim of abuse, crime or another traumatic event is a sensitive interest category. Google's examples are domestic abuse shelters and victim advocate services.
records.whatToDo: Sexual-abuse, domestic-violence and crime-victim campaigns should plan without remarketing or Customer Match.

records.policyName: Personalized advertising: Housing, Employment and Consumer finance (US and Canada)
records.rule: In the US and Canada, ads in housing, employment or consumer finance can't target by gender, age, parental status, marital status or ZIP code. Radius targeting of at least 1 km is allowed. Housing covers real estate services; employment covers job ads and hiring.
records.whatToDo: Target real-estate and debt-related campaigns by radius or city, not ZIP. Firm recruiting ads (hiring lawyers or staff) fall under employment.

records.policyName: Customer data policies: no sensitive conversion uploads
records.rule: Advertisers using enhanced conversions for web or for leads may not upload conversion information in sensitive categories. Google's list includes crime or alleged crime, divorce or separation, negative financial status, and health or medical information.
records.whatToDo: Before sending signed-case data back to Google, check whether the conversion itself reveals a sensitive fact (an arrest, a divorce, a bankruptcy, an injury). Ask Google or your counsel; don't assume it's allowed.
records.quote: You may not upload conversion information related to sensitive categories.

records.policyName: Customer Match policy: eligibility
records.rule: Any policy-compliant account with good payment history can use Customer Match for observation and exclusions. Using it for targeting and bid adjustments needs 90 days of account history and more than USD $50,000 lifetime spend. Only first-party data may be uploaded.
records.whatToDo: Firms below $50,000 lifetime spend can still upload past clients as exclusions. Never upload bought or shared lists. Sensitive practices can't use Customer Match for targeting at all (see the sensitive-category rows).
records.quote: If you have 90 days of Google Ads history and more than USD $50,000 total lifetime spend

sources.label: Google Ads policy: Customer Match policy
sources.quote: If you have 90 days of Google Ads history and more than USD $50,000 total lifetime spend

records.text: Any policy-compliant account with good payment history can use Customer Match for observation and exclusions. Using it for targeting and bid adjustments needs 90 days of account history and more than USD $50,000 lifetime spend. Only first-party data may be uploaded.

records.policyName: Trademarks
records.rule: Google doesn't restrict bidding on another firm's trademark as a keyword. If the owner complains, Google can restrict a competitor's use of that trademark in ad text.
records.whatToDo: Never put a rival firm's name in your ad text. Check your state's ethics rules before bidding on a rival's name; several states have opinions on it.
records.quote: Using trademarks in an ad from a direct competitor

records.note: Google's keyword stance doesn't settle the state ethics question (see our state rules dataset, 'Competitor names in ads').
records.text: Google doesn't restrict bidding on another firm's trademark as a keyword. If the owner complains, Google can restrict a competitor's use of that trademark in ad text.

records.policyName: Misrepresentation: Misleading representation
records.rule: Ads must not hide or misstate who the advertiser is or its qualifications. Google's own example: an affiliate marketer advertising legal services without saying it doesn't provide them.
records.whatToDo: Lead-generation and referral sites must say clearly that they are not a law firm. Firms must use their real name and real credentials.

sources.label: Google Ads policy: Misleading representation

records.text: Ads must not hide or misstate who the advertiser is or its qualifications. Google's own example: an affiliate marketer advertising legal services without saying it doesn't provide them.

records.policyName: Misrepresentation: Dishonest pricing practices
records.rule: Since October 28, 2025, advertisers must clearly show the payment model or full cost a user will bear, and bait-and-switch pricing is banned.
records.whatToDo: If your ad mentions price ('free consultation', 'flat fee', 'no fee unless we win'), make the landing page explain what the client pays and when.
records.quote: Advertisers must clearly and conspicuously disclose the payment model or full expense that a user will bear before and after purchase.

records.policyName: Editorial: phone numbers in ad text and business name
records.rule: Phone numbers can't go in ad text; use call assets instead. The business name field must be your domain or your recognized name, without promotional words. From October 2026 Google allows a business name that differs from the domain in limited verified cases.
records.whatToDo: Put the firm's real name in the business name field (not 'Top Injury Lawyers'). Put phone numbers in call assets.

records.policyName: Destination requirements: Unacceptable and unverified phone numbers
records.rule: Phone numbers in call-only ads, call assets and location assets must be verified, in service, local or domestic, and connect to the advertised firm. Fax, premium and vanity numbers are not acceptable. Since December 10, 2025, numbers tied to fraud or past violations are also unacceptable.
records.whatToDo: Use a real local or toll-free number that rings at your firm in call assets. Don't rely on a vanity number (letters) in call assets.

records.policyName: Data collection and use: inadequate data security
records.rule: Collecting sensitive numbers such as Social Security, driver's licence, national ID or healthcare numbers on a page without SSL is not allowed. Personal data must never be passed to Google in URLs or tags.
records.whatToDo: Serve every intake form over HTTPS, submit forms with POST, and keep names, emails and phone numbers out of URLs.

records.whatToDo: Appeal disapprovals as soon as they happen; don't leave old disapprovals sitting in the account.

records.policyName: Language targeting (Search)
records.rule: From September 2026, Search campaigns no longer have a campaign language setting. Google matches ads to the language of the search and the language of your ad.
records.whatToDo: Write separate Spanish ads (and Spanish landing pages) if you want Spanish searches. A Spanish campaign setting alone no longer does it.

records.policyName: Limited ad serving
records.rule: Google may limit impressions for advertisers it hasn't yet judged 'qualified', especially new or unbranded ones and those users report often. In 2026 Google extended this to Search and then to all Google Ads, rolling out gradually through 2028.
records.whatToDo: Complete advertiser verification, show your firm's own brand clearly in ads and on the landing page, and consider pinning your domain to headline 1.

records.policyName: Offline conversion imports through the Google Ads API
records.rule: Since June 15, 2026, the Google Ads API doesn't accept new users of offline conversion imports, including enhanced conversions for leads. New set-ups go through the Data Manager API. Conversions uploaded more than 90 days after the click aren't imported.
records.whatToDo: If you are starting to send signed cases back to Google, use Data Manager (or a CRM integration built on it). Upload within 90 days of the click.

records.whatToDo: If you test, bid on clicks and track consultations booked, not impressions.
records.quote: We recently launched Conversions API and pixel-based measurement

records.policyName: LinkedIn Advertising Policies
records.rule: LinkedIn has no restriction specific to legal services. Ads can't target on sensitive data, including criminal record, health and income, and affiliate advertising is prohibited.
records.whatToDo: LinkedIn suits business, employment-side and B2B practices; target by job and company, never by sensitive traits.
records.quote: data relating to a criminal record or alleged or actual commission of a crime
